answer.summary: Shaun Clowes’s core advice is to treat data as the prerequisite for useful LLM synthesis: gather broad, recent information about customers, their requests, and competitors, then supply it through your tools or workflow. Keep product work grounded in customer, market, and competitor perspectives, and be data-informed.

sections.heading: Give the LLM useful, current information
sections.content: Clowes describes an LLM as a synthesis machine: without data to synthesize, it has little to work with, and its output is only as good as the data it receives and how recent it is. For internal product work, gather as much relevant information as you can about customers, their asks, and competitors, bring it together, and provide it to the LLM—whether through your tooling, copy-and-paste, or another workflow. He says more information generally helps, while noting that this is not an absolute rule.

sections.heading: Keep the work anchored outside the company
sections.content: Clowes advises product managers to start from outside-the-building perspectives: in documents and other work, speak from the customer’s, market’s, and competitor’s points of view. He also recommends being data-informed. These habits complement LLM use by focusing the information and synthesis on market value rather than internal process.
